common_name: Joyce DeBaggio Rosemary (Golden Variegated Upright Rosemary)

planting.note: Set rooted cuttings out after the last frost into lean, fast-draining soil; keep this cultivar in the sunniest spot available, since full sun intensifies the gold leaf edging and shade causes it to fade toward plain green.

directions: Named for the wife of noted herb grower Thomas DeBaggio, this is an upright culinary rosemary whose needle-like leaves are edged in gold over green centers, giving the whole shrub a glowing two-tone look that is more pronounced on new growth. Pale blue flowers appear mainly in late winter and spring, though plants in mild climates may rebloom lightly through the year. Grow it in the same lean, well-drained, full-sun conditions as other upright rosemary types, and prune after flowering to keep the habit tidy, since variegated wood is somewhat less vigorous than plain green rosemary and benefits from avoiding hard renewal cuts. It can be used in the kitchen like any culinary rosemary but is most often grown as a specimen or hedge plant for its ornamental foliage.

common_name: Dancing Waters Rosemary (Arching Prostrate Landscape Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant on slopes, in rock walls, or at the edge of raised beds and containers where the trailing branches can cascade; give it the same gritty, fast-draining soil required by other prostrate rosemary types.

directions: Dancing Waters is a prostrate, Texas-recommended rosemary landscape selection with low, arching branches that trail over the ground or drape attractively over a wall or container edge rather than growing upright. It carries pale blue-purple flowers along the cascading stems and is grown chiefly for erosion control, slope planting, and softening hardscape edges rather than for cut-herb production. Site it in full sun with excellent drainage, since trailing rosemary forms are more prone to crown rot in heavy or poorly drained soil than upright types. Established plants need only occasional deep watering and tolerate heat and drought well once their roots are in.
sources: University of Tennessee Institute of Agriculture (UT Gardens)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into poor to average, sharply drained soil in full sun; this bushy, evenly rounded cultivar needs little staking or support compared with lankier upright types.

directions: Discovered as a chance seedling in the garden at Sissinghurst Castle, this cultivar forms a dense, evenly bushy, upright evergreen shrub that holds a neat rounded shape with minimal pruning. It is valued for an unusually heavy, rich-blue flower display in mid-spring that often continues sporadically through summer, and it has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its reliable garden performance. Both the aromatic foliage and the edible flowers can be used in the kitchen, and the long bloom period makes it a strong draw for bees. Grow it exactly as other upright culinary rosemary types, in lean, sharply drained soil with full sun exposure, and avoid wet winter soil, which is the main cause of losses.

common_name: Dutch Mill Rosemary (Extra Cold-Hardy Rounded Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; this is one of the more cold-tolerant rosemary selections, making it a candidate for gardens at the cool edge of rosemary's normal range where typical cultivars struggle to overwinter outdoors.

directions: Selected by grower Barbara Remington at the Dutch Mill Herb Farm in Forest Grove, Oregon, this cultivar forms a neatly rounded, well-proportioned shrub of fragrant medium-green foliage topped with light blue flowers each spring. It is notable among named rosemary cultivars for standing up to unusually cold winter temperatures that would kill many other selections outright, making it worth trying in gardens near the northern edge of what is normally considered rosemary-hardy territory. Otherwise it is grown like any upright culinary rosemary, in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, with light shearing after bloom to maintain its naturally tidy, rounded form. Established plants are drought-tolerant and need minimal supplemental water once settled in.

common_name: Mrs. Reed's Dark Blue Rosemary (Deep-Blue-Flowered Upright Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in lean, sharply drained soil; allow room for a fairly large bushy shrub, since this selection grows taller and wider than compact types like Blue Boy.

directions: This selection is grown chiefly for having some of the darkest, most saturated blue flowers of any rosemary cultivar, produced in the leaf axils in late spring and early summer against dense, dark green, needle-like foliage. It forms a large, bushy, evergreen shrub that is noticeably more vigorous and full-bodied than compact dwarf rosemary types, so give it generous spacing from the start rather than crowding it. Culture is otherwise standard for upright culinary rosemary: full sun, lean and sharply drained soil, and only occasional deep watering once established. Prune lightly after the main spring flush to maintain density and encourage continued branching.

common_name: Herb Cottage Rosemary (Cathedral Garden Culinary Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained soil; the tight, upright growth habit makes this a good choice for containers, small herb gardens, and narrow border plantings where a sprawling rosemary would be unwelcome.

directions: Herb Cottage originated at the Herb Cottage shop and garden associated with Washington National Cathedral and has since become a widely grown named selection valued for its tidy, tight-knit upright habit and dense, dark green foliage. Dark violet-blue flowers appear in late winter and early spring on wood from the previous season. Its high essential-oil content makes it a strongly flavorful choice for kitchen use, equal to or better than many standard culinary rosemary selections. Site it in full sun with sharp drainage and good air movement around the base, since crowded, poorly ventilated plantings are prone to fungal problems in humid Gulf Coast summers.

common_name: Mrs. Howard's Creeping Rosemary (Broad-Leaf Trailing Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant along border edges, in hanging baskets, or where the thick trailing stems can spill over a wall or container rim; use the same gritty, fast-draining soil required by other prostrate rosemary selections.

directions: Mrs. Howard's Creeping is a trailing rosemary distinguished from other prostrate selections by noticeably larger, broader leaves on thick cascading stems, giving it a coarser, bolder texture than finer-leaved creeping types. Light blue flowers appear in flushes through much of the year rather than in a single spring bloom, and the foliage carries a fuller, more traditional rosemary scent and flavor than many other trailing cultivars, making it useful in the kitchen as well as the landscape. It spreads quickly over a single growing season, so give it room to cascade over a wall, raised bed edge, or large container rather than crowding it among upright herbs. As with other prostrate rosemary types, full sun and sharply drained, lean soil are essential, and it performs best where winter temperatures stay above about 20°F.
